text.title: Grace
text.author: James Joyce
text.description: A man named Tom Kernan falls down the stairs at a bar while drunk and is rescued by friends. His companions—Mr. Power, Mr. Cunningham, and Mr. M'Coy—conspire to bring him to a Catholic retreat at a Jesuit church, where Father Purdon delivers a sermon on spiritual accounting for businessmen.

rootSpan.title: Grace
rootSpan.description: A man named Tom Kernan falls down the stairs at a bar while drunk and is rescued by friends. His companions—Mr. Power, Mr. Cunningham, and Mr. M'Coy—conspire to bring him to a Catholic retreat at a Jesuit church, where Father Purdon delivers a sermon on spiritual accounting for businessmen.

childSpans.title: The Fall and Rescue
childSpans.description: Tom Kernan falls down the stairs at a bar and is rescued by friends and strangers.

childSpans.title: The Accident in the Bar
childSpans.description: Two gentlemen discover Kernan at the foot of the stairs and attempt to help him.

childSpans.title: Discovery of the Injured Man
childSpans.description: Two gentlemen in the lavatory find Kernan collapsed at the foot of the stairs.

childSpans.title: The Crowd Gathers
childSpans.description: A ring of men forms around Kernan as the bar manager questions witnesses.

childSpans.title: The Constable Arrives
childSpans.description: A young constable enters and begins to take statements about the incident.

childSpans.title: Assistance and Departure from the Bar
childSpans.description: A young man in a cycling suit helps Kernan, and Mr. Power arrives to take him home.

childSpans.title: The Young Man's Assistance
childSpans.description: A young man in a cycling suit kneels beside Kernan and administers water and brandy.

childSpans.title: Mr. Power's Arrival
childSpans.description: Mr. Power appears and takes charge of Kernan, offering to see him home.

childSpans.title: Departure on Grafton Street
childSpans.description: The three men leave the bar and Kernan introduces himself as he boards a cab.

childSpans.title: Home and the Plot
childSpans.description: Kernan is brought home to his wife, and his friends conspire to bring him to a Catholic retreat.

childSpans.title: Kernan at Home
childSpans.description: Kernan is put to bed by his wife while Mr. Power speaks with the children.

childSpans.title: Arrival at Home
childSpans.description: The car halts at Kernan's house on Glasnevin Road and he is helped inside.

childSpans.title: Mrs. Kernan's Reaction
childSpans.description: Mrs. Kernan scolds her husband and reveals his drinking has been ongoing since Friday.

childSpans.title: Mr. Power's Promise
childSpans.description: Mr. Power promises to help reform Kernan and mentions talking to Martin Cunningham.

childSpans.title: Kernan's Recovery and the Plot Disclosed
childSpans.description: Kernan remains in bed for two days while his friends visit and disclose their plan for a retreat.

childSpans.title: Bed Rest and Recovery
childSpans.description: Kernan sends a letter to his office and remains in bed while his wife cares for him.

childSpans.title: Friends Visit the Bedroom
childSpans.description: Two nights after the accident, Cunningham, M'Coy, and Power visit Kernan in his bedroom.

childSpans.title: Discussion of the Accident
childSpans.description: The friends discuss Kernan's fall and his injured tongue, and Kernan mentions his companions.

childSpans.title: The Retreat Proposal
childSpans.description: The friends propose that Kernan join them on a retreat at a Jesuit church on Thursday.

childSpans.title: Discussion of the Jesuits
childSpans.description: The men discuss the Jesuit order and Father Purdon, who will lead the retreat.

childSpans.title: Theological Discussion and Fogarty's Visit
childSpans.description: The men engage in extended theological discussion about the Church, popes, and Catholic doctrine.

childSpans.title: Whisky and Theological Debate
childSpans.description: Mr. Fogarty arrives with whisky and the men discuss Pope Leo XIII and papal infallibility.

childSpans.title: Mr. Fogarty's Arrival
childSpans.description: Mr. Fogarty, a modest grocer, arrives with a gift of special whisky.

childSpans.title: Discussion of Pope Leo XIII
childSpans.description: The men discuss Pope Leo XIII's scholarship, poetry, and papal motto.

childSpans.title: Papal Infallibility Debate
childSpans.description: Cunningham recounts the story of the papal infallibility declaration and John MacHale's submission.

childSpans.title: Kernan's Memory of John MacHale
childSpans.description: Kernan recalls seeing John MacHale at the unveiling of Sir John Gray's statue.

childSpans.title: Retreat Confirmation and Candle Dispute
childSpans.description: Mr. Power announces the retreat plan to Mrs. Kernan and Kernan objects to using candles.

childSpans.title: Power Announces the Retreat
childSpans.description: Mr. Power tells Mrs. Kernan that they will make her husband a good Catholic.

childSpans.title: Kernan Objects to Candles
childSpans.description: Kernan refuses to use candles during the retreat, creating laughter among the group.

childSpans.title: The Retreat at the Jesuit Church
childSpans.description: The men attend the retreat at the Jesuit Church in Gardiner Street and Father Purdon delivers his sermon.

childSpans.title: Assembly at the Jesuit Church
childSpans.description: The men arrive at the Jesuit Church and take their seats in the transept.

childSpans.title: Arrival at the Church
childSpans.description: The men enter the transept of the Jesuit Church in Gardiner Street and find seating.

childSpans.title: Father Purdon's Sermon
childSpans.description: Father Purdon delivers a sermon on spiritual accounting for businessmen.

childSpans.title: Father Purdon Ascends the Pulpit
childSpans.description: Father Purdon climbs into the pulpit and the congregation kneels.

childSpans.title: The Sermon on Spiritual Accounting
childSpans.description: Father Purdon delivers his sermon using the metaphor of spiritual accounting for businessmen.

tom-kernan.name: Tom Kernan
tom-kernan.description: A commercial traveller of the old school who falls down the stairs while drunk and is subsequently brought to a Catholic retreat by his friends.
tom-kernan.context: A man of middle age who once had higher social standing but has declined due to drinking and poor business practices. He converted to Catholicism at the time of his marriage but has drifted from the Church.

data.physicalDescription: A man with a moustache, wearing a silk hat and gaiters. After his fall, his clothes are smeared with filth and blood trickles from his mouth. His tongue is injured.

mr-power.name: Mr. Power
mr-power.description: A younger man employed in the Royal Irish Constabulary Office in Dublin Castle who rescues Kernan and orchestrates the retreat plan.
textMentions: the young man in the cycling-suit
mr-power.context: A much younger man than Kernan who has risen socially while Kernan has declined. He is known for inexplicable debts but is well-liked and considered a good friend.

data.physicalDescription: A young man of fair complexion wearing a long yellow ulster.

mr-cunningham.name: Mr. Cunningham
mr-cunningham.description: An elder colleague of Mr. Power who is intelligent, sensible, and influential. He orchestrates the retreat plan and leads much of the theological discussion.
mr-cunningham.context: A thoroughly sensible man with natural astuteness from his work in police courts. He has studied philosophy and is considered a judge of character. His own marriage is unhappy as his wife is an incurable drunkard.

data.physicalDescription: A man whose face is said to resemble Shakespeare's.

mr-mcoy.name: Mr. M'Coy
mr-mcoy.description: A former tenor of some reputation who has had a varied career and is now secretary to the City Coroner. He participates in the retreat plan.
mr-mcoy.context: A man whose life has not followed a direct path. He has worked as a clerk, canvasser, town traveller, private inquiry agent, and in various other positions. His wife was a soprano and still teaches piano.

mrs-kernan.name: Mrs. Kernan
mrs-kernan.description: Tom Kernan's wife, an active and practical woman of middle age who manages the household and her husband's affairs with shrewdness.
mrs-kernan.context: A woman who has been married for twenty-five years and has raised three children while managing her husband's drinking and declining fortunes. She is pragmatic about religion and her husband's faults.

data.physicalDescription: A woman of middle age who has celebrated her silver wedding.

mr-fogarty.name: Mr. Fogarty
mr-fogarty.description: A modest grocer who failed in business as a licensed house keeper and now runs a small shop on Glasnevin Road. He visits Kernan and brings whisky.
mr-fogarty.context: A man of some culture and grace who has experienced business failure but maintains his dignity. He is interested in theological matters and papal history.

data.physicalDescription: A pale oval face with fair trailing moustache and fair eyebrows looped above pleasantly astonished eyes.

father-purdon.name: Father Purdon
father-purdon.description: A Jesuit priest who leads the retreat at Gardiner Street Church. He delivers a sermon on spiritual accounting for businessmen.
father-purdon.context: A Jesuit priest known for being a man of the world who understands the lives of businessmen. He is described as a jolly fellow with a red face.

data.physicalDescription: A powerful-looking figure with a massive red face, wearing a white surplice.

young-man-cycling-suit.name: Young Man in Cycling Suit
young-man-cycling-suit.description: An unnamed young man who assists Kernan after his fall by washing his wounds and administering brandy.
textMentions: the young man in the cycling-suit
young-man-cycling-suit.context: A compassionate stranger who happens to be at the bar and takes immediate action to help Kernan.

data.physicalDescription: A young man wearing a cycling suit.

bar-manager.name: Bar Manager
bar-manager.description: The manager of the bar where Kernan falls. He alerts the constable and investigates the incident.
bar-manager.context: A responsible official who takes charge of the situation and ensures proper authorities are notified.

constable.name: Constable

data.physicalDescription: A young man with thick immobile features.

mr-goldberg.description: A very fat short gentleman who is Harford's partner in the Liffey Loan Bank.
mr-goldberg.context: A Jewish businessman who partners with Harford in the Liffey Loan Bank.

e01.description: Two gentlemen discover Tom Kernan collapsed at the foot of the stairs in the bar lavatory, having fallen down the stairs while drunk.

e02.description: Two gentlemen and a curate carry Kernan upstairs and lay him on the floor of the bar. A ring of men gathers around him.

e03.description: The bar manager questions the crowd about Kernan's identity and companions. A curate mentions serving him rum. The manager asks if he was alone.

e04.description: The bar manager, alarmed by Kernan's pallor, sends for a policeman. A young constable arrives and begins to take statements.

e05.description: The constable asks who the injured man is and what his name and address are, but no one knows.

e06.description: A young man in a cycling suit kneels beside Kernan, calls for water, washes the blood from his mouth, and calls for brandy, which is forced down his throat.

e07.description: Mr. Power arrives at the bar, recognizes Kernan, and offers to take him home. The constable defers to Power's authority.

e08.description: Mr. Power takes Kernan's arm and asks if he can walk. The young man in the cycling suit takes his other arm and the crowd divides.

e09.description: The three men leave the bar. On Grafton Street, Mr. Power whistles for an outsider (cab). Kernan introduces himself as Kernan and thanks the young man.

e10.description: Kernan is hoisted onto the cab. As it passes Ballast Office, the clock shows half-past nine. Mr. Power examines Kernan's injured tongue with a match.

e11.description: The cab halts before a small house on the Glasnevin Road. Kernan is helped into the house by his wife.

e12.description: Mrs. Kernan scolds her husband, revealing he has been drinking since Friday. She speaks with Mr. Power about his friends and their influence on him.

e13.description: Mr. Power promises to help reform Kernan and mentions talking to Martin Cunningham about making him turn over a new leaf.

e14.description: Kernan sends a letter to his office and remains in bed. Mrs. Kernan makes beef-tea for him and scolds him. The narrative describes Kernan's character and business practices.

e15.description: Two nights after the accident, Cunningham, M'Coy, and Power visit Kernan in his bedroom. They discuss his injury and the plot to bring him to a retreat is revealed.

e16.description: The friends discuss Kernan's accident and his injured tongue. M'Coy asks if it pains him. Kernan mentions the companions he was with.

e17.description: Kernan mentions his companions: a little chap with sandy hair and Harford. Cunningham's reaction to the name Harford carries moral disapproval.

e18.description: The friends discuss the incident and the constable. They plan to meet on Thursday night at M'Auley's at half-seven for a retreat.

e19.description: The friends propose that Kernan join them on a retreat. Cunningham mentions Father Purdon and the Jesuits. Kernan listens with calm enmity.

e20.description: The men discuss the Jesuit Order, its history, and its merits. They praise the Jesuits as an educated order and discuss Father Purdon.

e21.description: Mr. Fogarty arrives with a gift of special whisky. He joins the company and sits with them on equal terms.

e22.description: The men discuss Pope Leo XIII's scholarship and poetry. Cunningham mentions his motto 'Lux upon Lux' (Light upon Light).

e23.description: The men continue discussing Pope Leo XIII's learning and poetry. Fogarty corrects Cunningham about the Pope's motto.

e24.description: Kernan asks about the popes and whether some were not respectable. Cunningham explains that no pope, however bad, ever preached false doctrine ex cathedra.

e25.description: Cunningham recounts the story of papal infallibility and John MacHale's submission. Kernan recalls seeing John MacHale at the unveiling of Sir John Gray's statue.

e26.description: Kernan describes seeing John MacHale at the statue unveiling and recalls his powerful gaze. He also mentions Crofton and Father Tom Burke.

e27.description: Mr. Power announces to Mrs. Kernan that they will make her husband a good Catholic. He reveals the retreat plan to her.

e28.description: Cunningham explains the retreat ceremony, including the renewal of baptismal vows with lighted candles. Kernan objects to using candles, creating laughter.

e29.description: The men arrive at the Jesuit Church in Gardiner Street for the retreat. The transept is nearly full with well-dressed businessmen. They take their seats.

e30.description: Father Purdon climbs into the pulpit. The congregation produces handkerchiefs and kneels. Father Purdon kneels, prays, and rises to address the congregation.

e31.description: Father Purdon delivers his sermon using the text about making friends out of the mammon of iniquity. He addresses businessmen and professional men, offering spiritual accounting as guidance.

Formalist Reading.name: Formalist Reading
Formalist Reading.description: A formalist interpretation of 'Grace' focusing on narrative structure, linguistic patterns, symbolic imagery, and the formal properties of the text itself. This reading emphasizes how Joyce's stylistic choices—including free indirect discourse, interior monologue, dialogue patterns, and symbolic objects—create meaning through form rather than external reference.

theme-fall-and-redemption.name: Fall and Redemption
theme-fall-and-redemption.description: The structural pattern of descent (physical fall down stairs) followed by attempted ascent (spiritual elevation through retreat). The narrative arc mirrors Christian redemption theology through formal repetition of falling/rising motifs.

theme-language-and-authority.name: Language and Authority
theme-language-and-authority.description: The formal properties of speech reveal power dynamics. Father Purdon's sermon, the constable's official discourse, and the friends' theological debate demonstrate how linguistic register and rhetorical authority construct social hierarchies and meaning.

theme-narrative-framing.name: Narrative Framing and Perspective
theme-narrative-framing.description: The story employs third-person limited perspective that shifts subtly between characters, creating ironic distance. The narrator's formal detachment from characters' self-deceptions generates meaning through the gap between what characters believe and what the narrative form reveals.

theme-ritual-and-form.name: Ritual and Formal Structure
theme-ritual-and-form.description: The retreat ceremony, the theological discussion, and even the accident itself are structured as formal rituals. The narrative form mirrors liturgical structure, with repetition, call-and-response patterns, and ceremonial progression creating meaning through formal arrangement.

sym-blood-medal.name: Blood Medal
sym-blood-medal.description: The dark medal of blood on the tessellated floor functions as a formal visual marker of the fall. Its geometric precision (medal-like shape on tessellated pattern) creates visual irony—the accident's violence rendered as aesthetic form.

currentMeanings.description: Mark of shame and degradation rendered as formal aesthetic object
Geometric pattern suggesting order imposed on chaos

sym-silk-hat.name: Silk Hat
sym-silk-hat.description: The silk hat that rolls away during the fall and is replaced on Kernan's head functions as a formal symbol of respectability and social position. Its displacement and restoration mirror the narrative's structural pattern of fall and attempted redemption.

currentMeanings.description: Marker of commercial traveller status and respectability
Object whose removal and replacement structures the narrative formally

sym-light-darkness.name: Light and Darkness
sym-light-darkness.description: The formal contrast between darkness (bar lavatory, Kernan's degradation) and light (church, candles, Father Purdon's sermon) structures the narrative visually and thematically. The red light before the altar and the lighted candles create a formal visual progression.

currentMeanings.description: Spiritual illumination and grace through formal visual contrast
Structural organizing principle dividing narrative into dark and light sections

sym-tongue-injury.name: Tongue Injury
sym-tongue-injury.description: Kernan's injured tongue functions as a formal symbol of silenced speech and compromised language. The repeated examination of the tongue (by Power with a match, in dialogue) creates a formal motif linking physical injury to linguistic disability.

currentMeanings.description: Physical manifestation of spiritual and moral damage
Impediment to authentic speech and self-expression

symrel-fall-grace.name: Fall as Prerequisite for Grace
symrel-fall-grace.description: The physical fall (e01) formally precedes and enables the spiritual grace of the retreat. The narrative structure itself enacts the theological paradox that degradation enables redemption.
symrel-fall-grace.nature: The formal sequence of events mirrors Christian theology: sin (fall) precedes grace (retreat). The narrative structure becomes a formal argument for redemption through degradation.
symrel-fall-grace.interpretation: The formal sequence of events mirrors Christian theology: sin (fall) precedes grace (retreat). The narrative structure becomes a formal argument for redemption through degradation.

symrel-light-purdon.name: Light and Father Purdon's Authority
symrel-light-purdon.description: The formal contrast between darkness and light culminates in Father Purdon's appearance in the pulpit, where light imagery concentrates. His linguistic authority is formally reinforced by visual symbolism.
symrel-light-purdon.nature: The formal arrangement of light imagery creates a visual hierarchy that mirrors the rhetorical authority of Father Purdon's sermon. Form and content align to reinforce institutional power.
symrel-light-purdon.interpretation: The formal arrangement of light imagery creates a visual hierarchy that mirrors the rhetorical authority of Father Purdon's sermon. Form and content align to reinforce institutional power.

symrel-tongue-sermon.name: Silenced Tongue and Purdon's Speech
symrel-tongue-sermon.description: Kernan's injured tongue contrasts formally with Father Purdon's eloquent sermon. The narrative structure creates ironic juxtaposition: the man who cannot speak properly listens to a priest who speaks with perfect authority.
symrel-tongue-sermon.nature: The formal contrast between Kernan's linguistic disability and Purdon's rhetorical mastery structures the power dynamics of the narrative. Language becomes the formal marker of authority and social position.
symrel-tongue-sermon.interpretation: The formal contrast between Kernan's linguistic disability and Purdon's rhetorical mastery structures the power dynamics of the narrative. Language becomes the formal marker of authority and social position.

narrator.name: Third-Person Limited Narrator
narrator.description: The narrator maintains formal distance from characters while occasionally employing free indirect discourse that reveals their consciousness. The narrative voice is detached and ironic, allowing readers to perceive the gap between characters' self-understanding and their actual circumstances. The narrator's formal restraint creates ironic effects through understatement and selective detail.

reader.name: Formalist Reader
reader.description: The reader is positioned to recognize formal patterns, structural repetitions, and symbolic arrangements. The reading experience depends on perceiving how Joyce's stylistic choices—dialogue patterns, narrative distance, symbolic imagery—create meaning through form. The reader must recognize irony generated by the gap between narrative form and character consciousness.

author.name: James Joyce
author.description: Joyce as a modernist formalist craftsman who constructs meaning through precise control of narrative structure, linguistic register, symbolic imagery, and formal arrangement. The author's primary concern is how form itself generates meaning, not external moral or social commentary.

e01.note: The initiating event that establishes the formal pattern of fall. The physical descent structures the entire narrative arc and introduces key symbolic imagery (blood medal, silk hat).

e02.note: Establishes the formal pattern of crowd gathering and collective response. Creates the social context for Kernan's degradation.

e03.note: Introduces formal dialogue patterns and the constable's official discourse. Establishes linguistic register as marker of authority.

e04.note: The constable's arrival introduces formal institutional language and power structures. His discourse contrasts with the informal speech of bystanders.

e05.note: Kernan's anonymity is formally significant—he is unknown, unidentified. This establishes his social marginality.

e06.note: The young man's assistance introduces the formal motif of care and recovery. His medical knowledge contrasts with the constable's bureaucratic approach.

e07.note: Mr. Power's arrival is formally significant as the first appearance of the orchestrator. His authority is established through the constable's deference.

e08.note: The physical support of Kernan by two men foreshadows the formal structure of the retreat—communal support and guidance.

e09.note: Kernan's introduction of himself marks a formal transition from anonymity to identity. The movement from bar to street establishes spatial progression.

e10.note: The examination of Kernan's tongue introduces the formal motif of linguistic injury. The clock showing half-past nine establishes temporal precision.

e11.note: Arrival at home marks formal transition from public to private space. Mrs. Kernan's appearance introduces the domestic sphere.

e12.note: Mrs. Kernan's scolding establishes her formal authority within the domestic sphere. Her speech contrasts with Mr. Power's diplomatic tone.

e13.note: Mr. Power's promise to reform Kernan formally announces the plot. The language of 'turning over a new leaf' introduces the redemption motif.

e14.note: The narrative description of Kernan's character and business practices provides formal character analysis. The beef-tea motif establishes domestic care.

e15.note: The friends' visit formally reveals the conspiracy to bring Kernan to the retreat. This is the structural turning point where the plot becomes explicit.

e16.note: Dialogue about the injury continues the formal motif of examining Kernan's damaged tongue. Establishes the conversational register of the friends.

e17.note: The mention of Harford introduces moral judgment through formal linguistic register. Cunningham's disapproval is conveyed through tone rather than explicit statement.

e18.note: The planning of the retreat is formally significant as the explicit statement of intention. The specific time and place establish formal structure.

e19.note: The proposal of the retreat to Kernan is formally crucial. His 'calm enmity' response reveals the ironic gap between his apparent acceptance and actual resistance.

e20.note: The theological discussion of the Jesuits establishes the formal register of educated discourse. The friends' knowledge is displayed through dialogue.

e21.note: Fogarty's arrival introduces a new character and the motif of gift-giving (whisky). His social status is established through formal description.

e22.note: The discussion of Pope Leo XIII's scholarship introduces formal intellectual discourse. The motto 'Lux upon Lux' introduces light imagery.

e23.note: Fogarty's correction of Cunningham establishes formal hierarchy of knowledge. The discussion continues the intellectual register.

e24.note: Cunningham's explanation of papal infallibility is formally significant as theological exposition. The formal language demonstrates institutional authority.

e25.note: The story of John MacHale and papal infallibility introduces historical formal narrative within the main narrative. Kernan's memory creates a nested structure.

e26.note: Kernan's recollection of seeing John MacHale establishes his participation in historical moments. The formal description of MacHale's 'powerful gaze' introduces visual symbolism.

e27.note: Mr. Power's announcement to Mrs. Kernan formally reveals the plot to her. The language of making Kernan 'a good Catholic' establishes the redemption goal.

e28.note: The discussion of retreat ceremony, particularly Kernan's objection to candles, is formally significant. His resistance creates ironic tension with the redemption narrative.

e29.note: The arrival at the church marks the formal transition to the climactic scene. The description of the transept filled with businessmen establishes the social context for the sermon.

e30.note: Father Purdon's ascent to the pulpit is formally climactic. The visual imagery of light and the formal ceremony establish the moment of spiritual authority.

e31.note: The sermon is the formal and thematic climax. Father Purdon's language of spiritual accounting and his address to businessmen create the final ironic statement of the narrative.

tom-kernan.note: The protagonist whose fall and attempted redemption structure the entire narrative. His character embodies the formal pattern of degradation and elevation.

mr-power.note: The orchestrator of the plot whose authority is established through formal linguistic register and social position. His role structures the narrative progression.

mr-cunningham.note: The intellectual authority figure whose theological discourse establishes the formal register of educated speech. His character demonstrates how language constructs authority.

father-purdon.note: The sermon-giver whose eloquence and formal authority represent the climactic moment. His language embodies institutional power.

mrs-kernan.note: The domestic authority figure whose scolding establishes the formal register of the home. Her character contrasts with the public sphere.

mr-mcoy.note: A participant in the plot whose varied career is formally significant as background. His character demonstrates social mobility through formal description.

mr-fogarty.note: The grocer whose arrival introduces a new formal register and the motif of gift-giving. His failed business career is formally relevant to the theme of redemption.

young-man-cycling-suit.note: The unnamed helper whose medical knowledge contrasts with other characters' responses. His anonymity is formally significant.

constable.note: The official whose bureaucratic discourse establishes formal authority through language. His character demonstrates institutional power.

mr-harford.note: The moneylender whose mention generates moral disapproval through formal linguistic register. His absence is formally significant.

bar-manager.note: The official whose response to the accident establishes institutional procedures. His character demonstrates formal authority.

john-machale.note: The historical figure whose story is nested within the narrative. His formal appearance in Kernan's memory creates narrative complexity.

pope-leo-xiii.note: The historical figure discussed in theological discourse. His motto 'Lux upon Lux' introduces light imagery formally.

kernan-children.note: Background figures whose presence establishes Kernan's domestic responsibilities. Formally significant as context for his character.

kernan-eldest-sons.note: Background figures whose successful placement establishes Kernan's family status. Formally significant as contrast to his decline.

abs-kernan-redemption.note: The central absence that drives the narrative. The desire for Kernan's spiritual redemption structures the entire plot and formal progression.

abs-kernan-dignity.note: Kernan's lost dignity is formally significant as the gap between his self-image and his actual social position. This gap generates irony.

abs-kernan-recovery.note: Physical recovery is formally significant as the prerequisite for spiritual recovery. The two are structurally linked.

abs-power-reform.note: Mr. Power's goal to reform Kernan is formally significant as the stated intention that drives the plot. It establishes the narrative's redemption structure.

abs-kernan-fear-of-candles.note: Kernan's resistance to candles is formally significant as the moment of ironic tension. His objection reveals the gap between acceptance and genuine conversion.

abs-kernan-drinking-problem.note: The underlying cause of Kernan's fall, formally significant as the unspoken problem that the retreat attempts to address. Its absence from explicit discussion is formally meaningful.

abs-mrs-kernan-patience.note: Mrs. Kernan's endurance is formally significant as the domestic counterpart to the public redemption narrative. Her patience structures the home sphere.

abs-cunningham-wisdom.note: Cunningham's wisdom is formally significant as the intellectual authority that guides the plot. His character embodies formal knowledge and linguistic mastery.

abs-kernan-acceptance.note: Kernan's acceptance of the retreat is formally significant as the apparent resolution. The irony lies in the gap between acceptance and genuine conversion.

span_1.note: The entire story maintains formal tension through the gap between surface narrative (redemption) and ironic subtext (questionable conversion).

span_2.note: The fall and rescue section establishes the formal pattern of degradation and assistance. High tension from the physical emergency.

span_3.note: The accident scene creates maximum formal tension through the contrast between Kernan's degradation and the crowd's response.

span_4.note: The discovery of the injured man establishes the initiating crisis. Maximum tension from the physical emergency.

span_5.note: The crowd gathering creates formal tension through collective response and the establishment of social context.

span_6.note: The constable's arrival introduces institutional authority and formal procedures. Tension shifts from physical emergency to bureaucratic response.

span_7.note: The assistance and departure section reduces physical tension while introducing the formal structure of rescue and care.

span_8.note: The young man's assistance creates formal contrast between medical knowledge and bureaucratic procedure.

span_9.note: Mr. Power's arrival introduces the orchestrator and reduces immediate tension through his authority.

span_10.note: The departure on Grafton Street marks transition from public emergency to private recovery. Tension decreases.

span_11.note: The home and plot section establishes the domestic sphere and reveals the conspiracy. Tension shifts from physical to social.

span_12.note: Kernan at home introduces Mrs. Kernan's authority and the domestic context. Tension from marital dynamics.

span_13.note: Arrival at home marks transition to recovery. Tension decreases as the immediate emergency passes.

span_14.note: Mrs. Kernan's reaction creates tension through her scolding and revelation of Kernan's chronic drinking.

span_15.note: Mr. Power's promise introduces the redemption plot. Tension shifts to social and spiritual concerns.

span_16.note: Recovery and plot disclosure section maintains tension through the revelation of the conspiracy and theological discussion.

span_17.note: Bed rest and recovery reduces immediate tension. The narrative provides character analysis and background.

span_18.note: Friends' visit creates tension through the revelation of the plot and Kernan's response.

span_19.note: Discussion of the accident maintains tension through dialogue and the introduction of moral judgment (Harford).

span_20.note: The retreat proposal creates tension through Kernan's 'calm enmity' response and the gap between acceptance and genuine conversion.

span_21.note: Discussion of the Jesuits establishes intellectual register. Tension decreases as the conversation becomes theological.

span_22.note: Theological discussion and Fogarty's visit section maintains moderate tension through intellectual discourse and the introduction of new character.

span_23.note: Whisky and theological debate section maintains tension through the formal register of educated discourse.

span_24.note: Fogarty's arrival introduces a new character and the motif of gift-giving. Tension decreases slightly.

span_25.note: Discussion of Pope Leo XIII maintains moderate tension through intellectual discourse and the introduction of light imagery.

span_26.note: Papal infallibility debate creates tension through formal theological exposition and the nested story of John MacHale.

span_27.note: Kernan's memory of John MacHale creates formal complexity through nested narrative. Tension maintained through historical reference.

span_28.note: Retreat confirmation and candle dispute section creates tension through Kernan's resistance and the gap between acceptance and genuine conversion.

span_29.note: Power's announcement of the retreat to Mrs. Kernan creates tension through the revelation of the plot.

span_30.note: Kernan's objection to candles creates ironic tension. His resistance reveals the gap between apparent acceptance and genuine conversion.

span_31.note: The retreat at the Jesuit Church section creates maximum tension through the formal structure of the climactic scene.

span_32.note: Assembly at the church creates tension through the formal description of the congregation and the establishment of the sacred space.

span_33.note: Arrival at the church marks the transition to the climactic scene. Tension maintained through formal description and social context.

span_34.note: Father Purdon's sermon section creates maximum tension through the formal and thematic climax.

span_35.note: Father Purdon's ascent to the pulpit creates tension through visual imagery and the establishment of spiritual authority.

span_36.note: The sermon on spiritual accounting is the formal and thematic climax. Maximum tension through the ironic address to businessmen and the final statement on grace.
